title: The Leadership Imperative: A Collaborative Approach to Professional Development in the Global Age of More for Less
author: Scott A. Westfahl · David B. Wilkins

st.an: The source accepts that Langdellian analytical education remains dominant but insufficiently adapted, and materially extends the reform case by advocating experiential complements and cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond the lawyer–nonlawyer divide.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source accepts that sophisticated in-house departments have shifted diagnosis, purchasing and work allocation toward corporate buyers while law firms remain important partners. It materially extends the cluster by identifying a specific interdependence: clients resist funding associate development but continue to rely on firms for trained lawyers who perform current work and later join legal departments.
qs: 71 Unsurprisingly, paying for the training and development of associates has been one of the primary targets of this budgetary axe.72 Companies do have a longterm interest in firms having well-trained associates, both to do their current work and because legal departments hire virtually all of their in-house lawyers from these institutions.73 We return to this point below.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s systemic account: the Cravath bargain depended on aligned training, promotion, client funding and low mobility, while modern partner insecurity, business-generation pressure, selective development and associate departures weaken apprenticeship. It materially extends that diagnosis by proposing shared responsibility among law schools, firms and corporate legal departments for transferable lawyer development.
qs: advocate for a system premised on the understanding of shared responsibilities among all relevant stakeholders for the training and development of lawyers rather than one that divides responsibilities among law schools, law firms, and clients.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source accepts that stronger corporate clients and the changing in-house sector have redistributed responsibility within corporate legal practice. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a collaborative professional-development model in which law schools, firms and corporate clients jointly cultivate competent and ethical lawyers, addressing the training and cultural consequences of buyer pressure rather than directly analysing professional capture or contextual regulation.
qs: advocate for a system premised on the understanding of shared responsibilities among all relevant stakeholders for the training and development of lawyers rather than one that divides responsibilities among law schools, law firms, and clients.

This means that law schools, law firms, and corporate clients have a mutual interest in ensuring that the next generation of lawyers will have the skills and disposition necessary to be competent and ethical corporate lawyers in the increasingly challenging legal market of the middle decades of the twenty-first century.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially develops it through a coordinated, lifelong model of lawyer development. It assigns shared responsibility to law schools, firms and corporate clients; preserves analytical training while adding adaptable professional skills and interdisciplinary relationships; proposes concrete experiential and team-based reforms; and acknowledges that its preliminary model lacks comprehensive validation and may require continued adaptation.
qs: 151 To be effective, this collaboration must concentrate on helping lawyers build three critical capacities: technical legal skills and expertise, professional skills that are adaptable to any professional context, and opportunity-generating networks of relationships.

As a first step, the narrow debates about who bears responsibility for what aspect of lawyer development need to turn to broader discussions around how law schools, law firms, and clients can collaborate and leverage each other’s strengths.

st.t: Legal education: Analysis should lose curricular dominance
st.an: The source accepts that rigorous legal analysis should be retained but no longer treated as the sole educational outcome. It materially extends that proposition by framing broader competence as collaborative, lifelong professional development spanning law school and practice, with interdisciplinary and leadership capabilities and sustained academic–practitioner involvement.
qs: Rather, at its heart, our model is about a shift in mindset away from believing that whether someone can “think like a lawyer”—and more specifically, think like a common law lawyer, as that is what is still predominantly taught—is the only law school outcome that matters.
And it must continue into the workplace, with the input and collaboration of academics who can help lawyers become lifelong learners.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s concern that changes to junior work can weaken apprenticeship and materially extends its redesign agenda with a shared development model spanning law schools, firms and clients. It contributes concrete institutional mechanisms—broader competencies, aligned incentives, feedback and adaptive coordination—rather than evidence about AI’s jagged capabilities or verification.
qs: There are several reasons why law schools and law firms in particular remain in denial about their failure to give young lawyers the broad professional skills and functioning opportunity-producing networks they need in a world in which the traditional patterns of apprenticeship and socialization have broken down.

Our hope is that moving from the divided Cravath model to our proposed shared model of lawyer professional development will build a foundation of communication, collaboration, and coordination that will make it far easier for law schools, law firms, and clients to adapt and align as those forces continue to require change.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts that sophisticated in-house lawyers are reshaping how legal services are sourced, delivered and priced, while materially extending the cluster’s training response: professional development should become a shared responsibility, with corporate clients partially funding collaborative reform rather than relying on junior billability to sustain apprenticeship.
qs: Just as the rise of sophisticated in-house lawyers has dramatically reduced the traditional information asymmetry between law firms and corporate clients regarding how legal services should be sourced, delivered, and priced, the burgeoning legal press has performed a similar function for today’s law students.

Throughout, we offer reasons why corporate clients should be willing to partially—but only partially—underwrite efforts to overcome resistance to change in law schools and law firms in order to reap the benefits that would flow from a new collaborative model of professional development.

st.t: Case teaching: Useful method became restrictive default
st.an: The source supports moving beyond the Langdellian model as legal education’s organising default. It argues that schools have made only marginal curricular and teaching changes despite shifts in practice, and it endorses cross-disciplinary professional development that crosses the lawyer–nonlawyer divide. The supplied evidence does not separately assess the case method’s analytical benefits, but it clearly supports the cluster’s reform direction.
qs: 1667 (2017)  importantly, notwithstanding the downturn in applications, few law schools have undertaken major changes to their curricula—and fewer still to their teaching methods—instead preferring to reduce enrollment while tinkering around the edges of what and how they teach.

As one of the Authors has written elsewhere, one of the things lawyers must learn to stop doing if they are to help their clients solve complex issues at the intersection of law, business, geopolitics, and other issues is dividing the world into “lawyers” and “nonlawyers.” Cf.

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central account: the Cravath model worked because its training system aligned with historically specific client, talent and organisational conditions, while modern firms retain its terminology and basic framework after the underlying relationships and development incentives have weakened. It also reinforces the cluster’s rejection of nostalgia about meritocracy and uniform lockstep governance.
qs: 60 But as the caveats and quotation marks in the above description underscore, the similarities between modern law firm practices and those of “golden age” firms are more symbolic than real.

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of an elevated in-house role, stronger client-side influence over law firms, and closer but more equal cooperation between general counsel and outside providers. Its discussion of recruiting experienced firm lawyers also supports increased in-house professional standing and career mobility. However, it offers only secondary citations and does not directly address the guardian-independence tension.
qs: For a comprehensive description of the evolution of the modern general counsel role and its contemporary significance, see HEINEMAN, supra note 69, at 3-8, which summarizes the transformation of the general counsel’s role both inside the company and outside in the legal profession and society as a whole.

kp.k: Technology does not eliminate the human-capital imperative
kp.d: The authors predict that corporate legal practice will remain a human-capital business for the foreseeable future despite technology's increasing importance. They explicitly decline to resolve whether AI-equipped clients will destroy the large-law-firm model or whether that model will remain resilient. Their contribution is a professional-development framework, not empirical evidence of AI displacement.
qs: Notwithstanding the growing importance of technology, the practice of law is—and is likely to remain for the foreseeable future—a human capital business.
In this Article, we do not seek to resolve these competing visions of the profession’s future.

kp.k: Shared development replaces the traditional division of responsibility
kp.d: The central recommendation is collaboration among law schools, law firms, and corporate clients throughout lawyers' careers. The authors argue that the historical allocation—schools teaching legal thinking, firms teaching practice, and clients funding training—is no longer aligned with clients' demand for multidisciplinary problem-solving and unwillingness to subsidize junior development.
qs: We advocate for a system premised on the understanding of shared responsibilities among all relevant stakeholders for the training and development of lawyers rather than one that divides responsibilities among law schools, law firms, and clients.
the model these parties are relying on to accomplish this goal is no longer fit for purpose.

kp.k: The Cravath model depended on mutually reinforcing institutions
kp.d: The historical account connects structured apprenticeship, homegrown partnership, up-or-out promotion, limited lateral mobility, and long-term client relationships. These arrangements allowed firms to recover training investments and pass costs to comparatively unsophisticated clients. The authors qualify the purported golden age by emphasizing exclusion and discrimination rather than treating it as universally beneficial.
qs: This system had three additional interlocking parts: training, promotion, and partnership.
law firms could pass most of the cost of whatever resources they did invest in training junior associates on to their clients.
this age was only “golden” for the select few who were allowed to participate.

kp.k: Mobility and competition undermine apprenticeship investment
kp.d: The authors identify rising competition for elite graduates, escalating salaries, lateral mobility, and increased associate-to-partner leverage as pressures on training. They report 385 U.S. firms with at least one hundred lawyers in 2016, while leading schools' graduating classes had not expanded correspondingly. Although leverage declined in many firms after the financial crisis, partners' business-generation pressures continued to weaken apprenticeship.
qs: in 2016 there were 385 U.S. law firms with at least one hundred lawyers

law firms pay significantly more for talent but have significantly less incentive to invest in the kind of apprenticeship training for the majority of their young lawyers on which the Cravath model of professional development depends.

The increase in the leverage ratio between associates and partners in many firms further exacerbated this trend, as increasingly busy partners found themselves responsible for the training (or at least supervision) of more and more junior associates.

kp.k: Sophisticated in-house buyers weaken client-funded training
kp.d: The article traces the growth of substantial corporate legal departments from the 1970s, accelerating in the final two decades of the twentieth century. General counsel increasingly diagnose legal needs, allocate work, and challenge outside fees, including training costs. The authors identify a tension between these short-term purchasing incentives and clients' longer-term reliance on trained firm associates as service providers and future in-house recruits.
qs: A key element of their new role is to reduce the price law firms charge for their services, particularly for work that does not directly benefit the client.

Companies do have a longterm interest in firms having well-trained associates, both to do their current work and because legal departments hire virtually all of their in-house lawyers from these institutions.

kp.k: Early specialization creates a self-reinforcing training decline
kp.d: The authors argue that price pressure encourages immediate associate specialization, eroding the generalist apprenticeship promise. Associates then leave earlier to avoid narrow career paths or obtain broader experience, further reducing firms' incentives to invest. Weaker partnership prospects and less secure partnership rewards compound this mechanism.
qs: Law firms have reacted to this downward price pressure by requiring associates to specialize immediately so as to make themselves productive as early as possible, further eroding the Cravath System’s promise of generalist training.
Both strategies in turn diminish the incentive for law firms—and even more for individual partners—to invest in the long-term development of associates

kp.k: Current success helps explain resistance to reform
kp.d: The authors acknowledge enduring strengths in analytical education, scholarship, academic independence, clinical offerings, and sophisticated corporate practice. Strong employment outcomes at elite schools and high firm profitability can obscure developmental weaknesses. They advocate preserving these strengths rather than wholesale replacement, while warning that competitive and client pressures make complacency increasingly dangerous.
qs: there are many aspects of the traditional model that do continue to work well and that provide law students with important skills
Given these important benefits, it is unsurprising that law schools have resisted calls for the wholesale overhaul of legal education.
And yet it is increasingly apparent that the status quo is unsustainable.

kp.k: Three capacities must develop across entire legal careers
kp.d: The proposed framework combines technical legal expertise, transferable professional skills, and opportunity-generating networks. These capacities should be developed together from law school through retirement, allowing lawyers to adapt, lead interdisciplinary work, and transition into public service or business. This is a normative model rather than a demonstrated intervention outcome.
qs: To be effective, this collaboration must concentrate on helping lawyers build three critical capacities: technical legal skills and expertise, professional skills that are adaptable to any professional context, and opportunity-generating networks of relationships.
These need to be developed at all stages of a legal career, from law school to retirement—and even beyond

kp.k: Law schools should deliberately teach leadership and collaboration
kp.d: The authors recommend team-based instruction, feedback tools, cross-cultural competence, strengths development, and supervised leadership experiences. They propose that at least one-third of courses, assignments, and assessments be team-based, while leaving institutions to decide whether reforms should be mandatory or elective. They explicitly acknowledge uncertainty about the effectiveness of their cross-cultural intervention and diversity training generally.
qs: Law schools should encourage faculty to have at least one-third of law school courses, assignments, and assessments be team-based
The jury is still out about the effectiveness of this particular intervention—and indeed of “diversity training” generally.
we bracket the question whether the reforms we seek should be made a mandatory part of the law school curriculum or instead offered as electives.

kp.d: Recommended educational additions include contextual problem-solving, negotiation, presentation, accounting, finance, valuation, technology literacy, design thinking, resilience, and mindfulness. Coding familiarity is proposed to help lawyers understand other professionals' methods rather than turn all lawyers into programmers. Design thinking should foster experimentation rather than immediate perfection.
qs: Law schools should engage in interdisciplinary efforts to help law students understand—and for some, learn to practice—basic coding and related technological skills.
The purpose of building these skills is not necessarily to develop the next generation of expert programmers.
how to prototype, experiment, and iterate when solving problems rather than expecting their first efforts to be perfect.

kp.k: Networks require deliberate teaching and institutional support
kp.d: The authors argue that competition within law school can obstruct enduring peer relationships. They recommend network-theory instruction, team projects, collaborative technology, and deliberate connections among students, faculty, and alumni. Firms and legal departments should similarly teach network mapping and recognize internal and external collaboration.
qs: The traditional legal education model too often fosters an unhealthy spirit of competition among classmates that impedes the building of effective networks.
Law schools could teach first-year students about network theory.

law firms and law departments should also provide specific training and workshop experiences to help lawyers understand how networks can help them maximize their opportunities and solve challenging problems.

kp.k: Other professions offer development and retention analogies
kp.d: Drawing on cited research and their professional experience, the authors contrast law firms with consulting, accounting, military, and technology organizations that invest systematically in development. McKinsey illustrates how substantial training and valued alumni networks may support loyalty and recruitment despite strict up-or-out rules. These are comparative examples, not controlled evidence that identical practices will work in law.
qs: McKinsey alumni are intensely loyal to the firm, even though its up-or-out process for associates is even stricter than that of most law firms.
What those organizations have realized is that their ability to compete in the market for clients depends almost exclusively on their ability to compete in the market for talent.
Google has an entire division dedicated to “People Analytics”

kp.k: Firms and clients should jointly fund development
kp.d: The authors reject both expecting clients to fund all training and clients' refusal to participate. They cite Intel's collaboration with its principal firms as an example: junior lawyers receive smaller matters to lead, opportunities to discuss legal developments, and feedback; firms reciprocate through briefings, feedback for in-house lawyers, and joint pro bono projects. The authors also recommend treating development as equal to or more important than client service.
qs: Law firms and clients should therefore invest together to create programs and practices in which both parties contribute to the training and development of the next generation of lawyers.

In this program, Intel invests in developing junior lawyers by giving them smaller cases to lead, inviting them to give “fireside chats” on developing legal issues, and providing feedback to associates and firm leaders about their development.
Fundamentally, law firms and in-house legal departments need to consider leadership and talent development as equal to or even more important than client service

kp.k: Measurement should extend beyond billing to developmental quality
kp.d: The authors criticize evaluation and reward systems centered on hours billed and realization. They recommend transparent competency expectations, engagement measurement, tracking professional skills, and evaluating team processes as well as client outcomes. Formal assignment systems and learning records should address developmental gaps and the risks of favoritism and unconscious bias in free-market staffing.
qs: productivity—measured by hours billed and realization rate—is the only real metric that matters.

Rather than caring only about what results are achieved for a client at the end of the day, law firms also need to focus attention on how well their lawyers have collaborated and worked together as a team.

What is typically missing, however, is an organized way of tracking what a lawyer has already learned—or still needs to learn—and a formal work assignment system ensuring that on-the-job training aligns most effectively with a lawyer’s development needs.

kp.k: Inclusive development requires structural change and sponsorship
kp.d: The authors argue that unequal access to training, bias, harassment, and barriers to leadership undermine the profession's talent model, particularly for women and lawyers of color. Recommendations include rotating leadership roles, reconsidering election arrangements, stronger action against discriminatory behavior, transparent metrics, and sponsorship that requires senior lawyers to actively champion juniors rather than merely advise them.
qs: law firms and their clients need to take a long, hard look at the systems, structures, and cultural barriers to progress in this area.
law firms should consider developing a cultural expectation around the rotation of leadership roles.
Unlike mentorship, sponsorship requires senior lawyers to put their personal reputations on the line for younger lawyers and be their internal and external champions.

kp.k: Leadership development needs training, feedback, and early responsibility
kp.d: The authors recommend leadership training every year and a half to two years for associates, including three- to seven-day cohort programs, and staged training for partners entering progressively larger roles. They propose developmental upward feedback with coaching, while acknowledging confidentiality concerns and poorly implemented reviews. Juniors should receive supervised leadership opportunities without assuming responsibility for major engagements beyond their competence.
qs: Typically, that means every year and a half to two years for a law firm associate.
intense, executive educationtype programs that are three to seven days long for cohorts of similarly tenured associates.
We suggest that law firms and in-house legal departments start simply by instituting upward feedback for developmental purposes only, ideally in conjunction with leadership training.
Law firms should proactively coordinate and provide leadership experiences that give associates and partners early, supervised opportunities to grow and learn as leaders.

kp.k: Protected research investment could support collaborative innovation
kp.d: The authors propose offsite research-and-development labs where selected associates and partners learn design thinking and address organizational or client problems across offices and seniority levels. Clients could join through secondments. They recommend a fixed multiyear capital commitment rather than a discretionary annual budget vulnerable to cuts.
qs: Partners and associates showing leadership potential could be seconded to an offsite R&D lab to learn design thinking principles and work across offices, departments, and hierarchical levels to address key organizational and client issues.

Funding for the R&D lab should be treated as a capital investment, with an allocated fixed annual budget like a real estate lease over a period of years rather than a budget that can easily be slashed from year to year.

kp.k: Continuous realignment remains necessary as technology changes
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that even full adoption would not ensure permanent alignment. Globalization and technology could make their proposed arrangements obsolete, just as changed market conditions undermined the Cravath system. Their qualified hope is that shared responsibility and sustained communication will improve adaptive capacity; failure to improve development risks talented people choosing other careers.
qs: there is a real danger that the new models that law schools, law firms, and clients might put into place could become similarly obsolete as the rapid pace of large-scale forces like globalization and technology shift the legal landscape.
Our hope is that moving from the divided Cravath model to our proposed shared model of lawyer professional development will build a foundation of communication, collaboration, and coordination

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Westfahl and Wilkins predict that corporate legal practice will remain a human-capital business despite technology’s growing importance; they do not advance a specific AI-displacement prediction.
pts.d: The authors’ affirmative position is that technology does not eliminate firms’ need to recruit, develop, retain, and deploy talented lawyers. The introduction raises the possibility that in-house departments using big data and AI could destabilize or destroy the traditional large-law-firm model, but presents this as an unresolved debate, not the authors’ prediction. Their further technology-related claim is a conditional warning: continuing technological and global change could render even their proposed professional-development arrangements obsolete. They hope shared responsibility among law schools, firms, and clients will improve adaptability. These are broad technology-related claims, not claims about particular AI capabilities or measured automation effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology-related predictions rest on institutional analysis and historical analogy, not AI-specific empirical testing.
pts.d: The article supports its professional-development argument with historical accounts of the Cravath System, research on legal careers and markets, and the authors’ research and executive-education experience. Its warning about future obsolescence draws an analogy to the breakdown of the traditional model as client markets, talent markets, and firm organization changed. It offers no AI-specific benchmark, adoption study, productivity measurement, or employment estimate establishing either continued human centrality or future technological disruption. Authorities predicting technology-driven elimination of lawyers’ jobs appear as background to the debate the authors expressly decline to resolve.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Human centrality is forecast for the unspecified “foreseeable future” from 2017; possible technological obsolescence concerns the coming decades.
pts.d: The authors provide no dated AI-adoption or displacement milestone. Their expectation of continued reliance on law graduates is qualified by possible relaxation of restrictions on nonlawyer ownership and participation. Their warning about professional-development models becoming obsolete applies even if institutions adopt all their recommendations. Greater adaptability through collaboration is expressed as a hope rather than a guaranteed outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate law firms, future lawyers, law schools, and corporate legal departments.
pts.d: Continued human centrality means firms must sustain talent investment while delivering value to increasingly sophisticated corporate clients. Law schools, firms, and buyer-side legal departments share an interest in preparing lawyers for changing practice conditions. The authors propose technical expertise, transferable professional skills, and interdisciplinary networks as preparation for adaptation. They do not specify AI-driven headcount losses, changes in staffing shape, task substitution, or access-to-justice effects.
